lines.text: There is a kind of honesty that doesn't wait for good news first.
Habakkuk stood on a hillside and named every loss out loud.
The fig tree will not blossom. No fruit in the vines.
The labour of the olive has failed, and the fields have nothing to give.
The flock is cut off from the fold. The stalls stand empty.
No denial. No spiritualizing. Just the truth, spoken plainly.
And then, in the very next breath, the turn.
Yet I will rejoice in the Lord.
I will joy in the God of my salvation.
Not because the vine finally budded. It hadn't.
Habakkuk didn't wait for his bank account to recover before he decided to rejoice.
He separated his joy from his receipts while the receipts were still on the table.
That's not denial. That's an anchor dropped somewhere the storm can't reach.
Across the Bible, in another ruin, Job is sitting in the wreckage of everything he owned.
Ash on his skin. Grief in his posture.
And still he says the sentence that outlives every other line he ever spoke.
Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
No explanation required. Trust was never waiting on a memo from heaven.
Centuries later, a king lies awake, alone, talking to the one person who won't talk back.
David turns and interrogates his own soul.
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? Why art thou disquieted within me?
He doesn't ask his soul for permission. He issues it a command.
Hope thou in God.
Three men. Three ruins. The same radical move.
None of them waited for the circumstance to change first.
None of them waited for the feeling to catch up first.
Your rejoicing was never supposed to be a reaction.
It was always meant to be a decision.
The will moves first. The feeling is left to catch up later.
So here's the real question tonight.
What's your empty vine right now?
What are you still waiting to change before you'll let yourself rejoice?
Stop listening to your soul, and start talking to it.
Preach to it until it believes you.
The Lord God is my strength.
He will make my feet like hinds' feet.
And He will make me walk upon my high places.
In Jesus' name, amen.

title: Word and Faith Network
subtitle: Preach to Your Own Soul
story: Habakkuk, Job, and David all stood in a ruin and did the same radical thing: they rejoiced before anything changed. Rejoicing was never a reaction to good news - it's a decision the will makes first, and lets the feeling catch up later.
